absent: Bounce slot search, alignment offset derivation, slot release, pool creation and deferred free scheduling details are absent.
Direct address translation, coherence test, protection selection and coherent pool mapping helpers are absent.
Benchmark harness loop, timing accumulation, ioctl dispatch and debug entry lifecycle are absent.
Architecture synchronization, encryption capability queries and system RAM walk helpers are absent.
Scatter table, page allocation and device logging internals are absent.

findings.text: Bounce buffer mapping exposes allocation, release and size query entry points that translate an original physical address into a bounce address, undo such a translation with direction aware synchronization, and report the largest mappable span after alignment penalties.

Direct mapping exposes helpers to build a scatter table, test mappability, establish a user mapping, test mask support, test full RAM coverage, report maximum span, test sync need and install a sole offset range.
Mapping layer exposes addressing limit test and required mask query that guide choice of mapping path from masks and coverage.
Dummy operations table provides failing handlers for all mapping callbacks, offering a safe placeholder where direct mapping is unavailable.

Bounce allocation rejects calls when pool memory is missing or empty, when guest encryption state mismatches pool sharing state, and when host encryption requires shared pools but the pool is private, while forcing the sharing attribute to match pool kind and warning once about oversized alignment or memory encryption use.

On success the allocator derives an alignment offset from device and original address, rounds the request to alignment granularity, locates free slots, records per slot origin and leading pad count, and always pre copies the original range into the bounce area so partial device writes preserve untouched bytes.

Bounce copy resolves slot state from bounce address, skips invalid origins, flushes for incoherent device to memory transfers, adjusts for alignment offset, truncates overlong requests with a warning, and moves data either page wise under interrupt protection for high memory or by direct memory copy otherwise, clearing sanitizer state on device to memory paths.

Unmapping synchronizes back to the original only when skip sync is clear and direction allows device writes, then either destroys a transient pool and accounts its slabs or releases the slots for reuse.

Transient handling has build dependent forms where a form detects transient pools, updates usage counts and removes the pool while the alternate form is inert, with matching active and inert forms for the transient usage counter.
Used capacity is reported either from a high water counter when debug tracking is enabled or by summing per area usage across either a sole default pool or a dynamic pool list.

Scatter table creation builds a sole entry from the direct page with page rounded length, mappability depends on coherence or on a build option for incoherent mapping, and user mapping applies device specific protections, prefers coherent pools, validates page offsets against the mapping length and remaps the corresponding frame range.

Mask support accepts any sufficiently wide mask and otherwise compares against the smallest of physical memory and zone limits after unencrypted translation, range lookup scans the device range map by frame number, full RAM coverage walks all RAM checking each span has a range entry, and maximum span delegates to bounce limits only when bounce is active and needed.

Addressing is deemed limited when effective mask falls below required mask, required mask favors direct needs when direct allocation applies and otherwise falls back to narrow defaults or operation provided values, and the direct path is taken when no translation is in use and either no custom operations exist or bypass is enabled with sufficient mask.
Bounce maximum span starts from segment count times slot size and subtracts a penalty derived from the device minimum alignment mask rounded to slot granularity.

Synchronization is required for incoherent devices or when the address resolves inside a bounce pool, and offset setup rejects devices that already carry a range map, ignores absent shift and otherwise installs a sole range entry describing the shift between processor and bus views.

Scatter list synchronization and release helpers for the direct path are inert, while single synchronization initially synchronizes any bounce state then performs architecture specific device synchronization and flush for incoherent devices.
Dummy handlers fail user mapping and single mapping, reject scatter mapping, report no mask as supported, and warn if either release path is ever invoked since successful mapping is impossible.

Benchmark defines single page run and scatter run parameter blocks where a granule controls either page count or entry count, preparation allocates buffers and tables with cleanup on failure, initialization stains buffers with a fixed fill except for device to memory runs, and mapping uses the standard single and scatter mapping calls with error logging.

Pool removal serializes list unlinking with the device bounce lock held with interrupts saved, followed by deferred reclamation outside the lock, while dynamic usage summation walks the pool list under read side protection and high memory bounce copies protect each page access with interrupt save and restore.
Benchmark run state holds parameters, target device, debug entry, transfer direction and atomic accumulators for mapping timing, unmapping timing, squared timings and loop counts.
Benchmark operations bundle groups callbacks for preparation, cleanup, data initialization, mapping and unmapping so single and scatter modes share a common driver loop.

Single mode parameters carry device, mapped address, contiguous buffer, page count and direction, while scatter mode parameters carry a table, device, page count, direction and a flexible trailing array of per entry buffers sized by page count.

Bounce slot lifecycle progresses from free to allocated with recorded origins and pad, then usable for device transfer with pre and post synchronization, ending in either slot release for persistent pools or whole pool destruction with usage accounting for transient pools.
Benchmark iteration progresses through allocate, stain, map, unmap and free, where allocation failure aborts the run and unmapping always follows a successful mapping before buffers are released.

Direct user mapping and dummy mapping handlers serve as address space operation callbacks that validate offsets and either establish a frame remapping or fail, forming the user visible mapping entry surface.
Benchmark single and scatter callback sets provide the mode specific implementations invoked by a common harness loop for setup, data preparation, timed mapping and teardown.

Exhausted bounce capacity, encryption pool mismatches and missing pools all surface as mapping errors with rate limited diagnostics, and oversized alignment can make near maximum requests unsatisfiable.

Mismatched mapping length versus allocation length triggers truncation with a warning rather than overflow, invalid slot origins cause silent skip, and sanitizer checks for outgoing data are deliberately omitted to avoid false alarms on uninitialized device target buffers.
Repeated offset installation, out of range page offsets and unsupported masks are rejected without side effects, while dummy release paths warn because they indicate a logic error if ever reached.
Benchmark logging prefixes messages with the module name and the direct header defines a once only inclusion guard.
